title: Trump Allies Circulate Draft Election Emergency Order; Trump Says He Is Not Considering It
description_short: PBS reported a 17-page draft order among Trump allies proposed emergency powers over the 2026 midterms; Trump said he was not considering declaring an emergency.
description_medium: PBS News reported on February 27, 2026, that a 17-page draft executive order circulating among Trump allies proposed declaring a national emergency to expand federal control over parts of the 2026 midterm elections. The draft included hand-counting and voter-identification provisions. PBS reported that Trump said he was not considering declaring an emergency around the midterms. The source describes a proposal, not an order Trump enacted.
description_long: On February 27, 2026, PBS News reported that a 17-page draft executive order was circulating among Trump allies. PBS said it reviewed the working document. The draft proposed declaring a national emergency and using it to assert federal control over parts of the 2026 midterm election process. Provisions described by PBS included hand-counted ballots, voter identification, and voter re-registration with proof of citizenship. The article presented these as elements of a proposal, not as changes that had taken effect. PBS reported that Trump said he was not considering declaring a national emergency around the midterms; in his reported response to a question about the draft, he said, “Who told you that?” Peter Ticktin, a Trump ally, confirmed to PBS that the draft had circulated among some supporters. The record therefore concerns circulation of a draft by allies and public reporting about Trump’s response. It does not establish that Trump ordered the draft, adopted it, deployed National Guard troops at polling places, or changed election administration under it. This entry makes no claim that the draft was enacted or implemented.

title: Trump Administration Asked Senior Security Job Candidates Questions About January 6
description_short: The Washington Post reported yes-or-no political questions for top intelligence and law-enforcement candidates, including whether January 6 was “an inside job.”
description_medium: On February 8, 2025, The Washington Post reported that candidates for top intelligence and law-enforcement positions in the Trump administration were asked yes-or-no questions about the 2020 election and January 6, including whether January 6 was “an inside job.” The report said the questions appeared designed to test candidates’ acceptance of the president’s claims. It does not describe signed oaths imposed on career employees.
description_long: The Washington Post reported that candidates for top intelligence and law-enforcement jobs in the Trump administration faced yes-or-no questions about the 2020 election and its aftermath. One example was whether January 6 was “an inside job.” The article said the questions appeared designed to determine whether candidates had embraced President Trump’s false claims about the election, citing people familiar with screening cases. The report concerns candidates for senior national-security posts, not a government-wide requirement that career employees sign personal loyalty statements. The supplied frozen card asserted such oaths, refusals, and administrative leave, but the accessed reporting does not establish those claims. This repaired entry is limited to the interview-screening questions described by the Post. It does not claim that every nominee received the questions, that the questions were written or ordered personally by Trump, that a candidate was rejected for an answer, or that employees were required to swear loyalty to him. The article path dates the report to February 8, and its extracted page states it was updated February 9, 2025.

title: Education Department Announces Reduction Affecting 1,315 Employees
description_short: On March 11, 2025, the Education Department announced a reduction affecting nearly half its workforce; ABC News reported notices to 1,315 employees.
description_medium: On March 11, 2025, the Department of Education announced a reduction in force affecting nearly half its workforce. The department’s release said its total workforce would fall from 4,133 at inauguration to roughly 2,183 after the action. ABC News reported that notices went to 1,315 employees; affected staff were set to enter administrative leave on March 21. The accessed sources do not establish direct DOGE direction.
description_long: The Department of Education announced a reduction in force on March 11, 2025. Its release said the action would affect nearly 50 percent of the department’s workforce and that impacted staff would be placed on administrative leave beginning March 21. The department listed 4,133 employees when President Trump took office and roughly 2,183 after the action; it said nearly 600 employees had already accepted voluntary resignation or retirement opportunities during the prior seven weeks. ABC News reported that reduction-in-force notices went to 1,315 employees on March 11 and that those affected were set to enter administrative leave on March 21, with pay and benefits through June 9. The department described the action as part of its “final mission.” This repaired account records the department’s announced workforce reduction and reported scale. The sources do not establish that DOGE directly ordered or carried out the reduction, so the frozen card’s DOGE attribution is omitted. The accessed sources also do not support the frozen card’s claims that particular program offices lost all staff, that compliance contacts disappeared, that complaints accumulated without staff, or that teachers unions called the action sabotage.

title: Unverified Supplied Allegation: FBI Monitoring of Mosques Under Kash Patel
description_short: Internal, unverified draft of the supplied allegation that the FBI resumed mosque monitoring under Kash Patel; the alleged program has not been independently established.
description_medium: The supplied record alleges that, beginning in March 2025, the FBI under Director Kash Patel restarted monitoring of mosques and Muslim community organizations. It describes agents attending sermons, tracking worshippers, and recruiting informants. Those actions, their scale, and the alleged program are unverified in the evidence available for this draft. This is an internal rendering of the supplied allegation, not a finding or publication-ready account.
description_long: According to the unverified allegation in the frozen record, FBI Director Kash Patel’s bureau supposedly resumed a program targeting mosques and Muslim community organizations in March 2025. The supplied account claims agents were assigned to monitor sermons, record attendees, and recruit informants in Muslim communities around the country. It characterizes the alleged activity as religious profiling that would raise First Amendment concerns. The text compares it with surveillance practices after September 11 and states that Muslim civil-rights organizations condemned the alleged return to that approach. It also claims earlier religious profiling produced no actionable intelligence. These are allegations stated in the supplied record, not findings or corroborated events. The record provides no named agency directive, case number, affected mosque, quoted organizer, named source, or underlying document to establish when any monitoring occurred, who authorized it, how many people or communities were affected, or whether informants were recruited. The scope, method, duration, constitutional consequences, and asserted lack of intelligence value remain unresolved. The copy is retained only as an internal draft of the allegation, with publication eligibility turned off until evidence supports the core event.
